extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and supervisory patent examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for USPTO examiners on how to examine patent applications, determine and articulate rejections (especially under 35 U.S.C. §§101, 102, 103), and use Patentability Report procedures. Covers procedural handling, prior art selection, effective filing date determination, and treatment of form defects and abstracts/foreign documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Patentability Report practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentability Report practice is not obligatory and should be resorted to only where it will save total examiner time or result in improved quality of action due to specialized knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentability Reports are appropriate when plural, indivisible inventions are claimed and specialists on each character of the claimed invention treating claims in their specialty will save time or improve quality. Not proper where claims are directed to the same character of invention but differ in scope only. Examples where P.R. is ordinarily not proper: (A) claims related as manufacturing process and product defined by the process; (B) product and process where process merely makes a product with certain characteristics; (C) combination vs subcombination distinguished solely by characteristics of the subcombination. A P.R. that will save total examiner time requires approval of the Director of the Technology Center and the “Approved” stamp on the memorandum requesting the P.R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence of Examination in P.R. cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When supervisory patent examiners involved in a Patentability Report (P.R.) case cannot agree on the order of examination by Technology Centers (TCs), the supervisory examiner having jurisdiction will direct a complete search of the art relevant to his or her claims prior to referring the application to another TC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The TC to which the application is referred must be advised of the results of this search. If supervisors believe a different sequence of search is expedient, the order should be modified accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting and Recording Patentability Reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Forwarding an application for a Patentability Report is not to be treated as a transfer by the forwarding TC; when P.R. is completed and application returned it is not counted as a receipt or action by transfer, though credit is given for time spent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The date status of the application in the reporting TC is determined on the basis of the dates in the TC of original jurisdiction. Timely reminders should be furnished to the TC making the P.R. to ensure orderly progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicate prints of drawings for P.R. applications
rubrics_metrics.description: In Patentability Report applications having drawings, the assigned examiner will furnish the reporting Technology Center prints of the applicable drawing sheets for interference search purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate that duplicate prints were provided (e.g., pencil notation on file wrapper). Upon allowance or abandonment, notify reporting TCs at once; reporting TC examiners should note allowance/abandonment dates on duplicates. Duplicate prints may be destroyed when of no value to reporting TC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviews with applicants in P.R. cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When an interview is held on an application for which a Patentability Report has been adopted, the reporting Technology Center may be called on for assistance when the interview concerns claims treated by them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 713–§ 713.10 for general interview procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goal and nature of examination
rubrics_metrics.description: After reading the application and understanding the claimed invention, the examiner makes a prior art search and reviews the application with the state of the prior art to determine whether the claims define a useful, novel, nonobvious, and enabled invention clearly described in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goal is to clearly articulate any rejection early in prosecution so the applicant can respond; the examiner must review all evidence (including applicant arguments) before the next Office action. If information reasonably necessary for examination should be required from applicant under 37 CFR 1.105, generally make such a requirement prior to or with the first Office action on the merits and follow MPEP § 704.10 et seq. Examiners should not overlook allowing claims that properly define the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection requirements under 37 CFR 1.104
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention is not considered patentable as claimed, the claims (or those considered unpatentable) will be rejected. When rejecting for lack of novelty or obviousness, the examiner must cite the best references at hand and, if a reference is complex or shows other inventions, designate the particular part relied on 'as nearly as practicable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pertinence of each reference must be clearly explained and each rejected claim specified. Examiner may rely upon admissions by applicant or facts within examiner's knowledge. Subject matter developed by another person that qualifies as prior art only under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) or (g) may be used under 35 U.S.C. 103 unless entire rights were commonly owned or subject to obligation of assignment. Claims precluded by waiver in a published statutory invention registration must be rejected as specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform application of patentability standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards of patentability (novelty, usefulness, unobviousness under 35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103) must be the same throughout the Office; an application should not be allowed unless and until issues pertinent to patentability have been raised and resolved during examination and prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the 'preponderance of the evidence' test: an examiner should reject a claim if, in view of prior art and record evidence, it is more likely than not that the claim is unpatentable. The mere fact a claim is a 'picture' of the invention is not justification for allowance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive handling of form defects or omission of a limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: When patentable subject matter is disclosed and claims are intended to be directed to such subject matter, but are unallowable due to defects in form or omission of a limitation, the examiner should not stop with a bare objection or rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner's action should be constructive and, when possible, offer a definite suggestion for correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter disclosed but not claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner is satisfied after search that patentable subject matter has been disclosed and the applicant intends to claim it, the examiner may note in the Office action that certain aspects or features have not been claimed and that if properly claimed such claims may be given favorable consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Office action to inform applicant of unclaimed patentable aspects to encourage appropriate claiming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsideration after reply by applicant (37 CFR 1.112)
rubrics_metrics.description: After reply by applicant or patent owner to a non-final action (and any inter partes comments), the application or patent under reexamination will be reconsidered and again examined; applicant will be notified if claims are rejected, objections made, or decisions favorable to patentability are made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may reply as provided in §§ 1.111 or 1.945 with or without amendment unless the Office action is made final (§ 1.113), an appeal has been taken (§ 1.191), or other specified closing actions have occurred. Once an appeal is taken, amendments are subject to 37 CFR 1.116(b) and (c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between rejections and objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusal to grant claims because the subject matter as claimed is considered unpatentable is a 'rejection.' If the form of the claim is improper (distinct from substance), an 'objection' is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejections (merits) are subject to review by the Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences; objections (formal matters) generally are reviewable only by petition to the Commissioner. Formal matters should not be combined in appeals to the Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection on prior art is the most frequent ground (102/103)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most frequent ground of rejection is unpatentability in view of the prior art — either lack of novelty under 35 U.S.C. 102 or obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language in rejecting claims should be unequivocal. See MPEP § 707.07(d) for language guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of prior art; use best available art
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art rejections should ordinarily be confined strictly to the best available art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions where other references may be used include: (A) propriety of a 102 or 103 rejection depends on particular interpretation of a claim; (B) a claim is met only in terms by a reference which does not disclose the inventive concept; (C) the most pertinent reference seems likely to be antedated by a 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit/declaration. Avoid merely cumulative rejections and back up exceptions with the best other art available. See MPEP § 707.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance upon abstracts and foreign-language documents
rubrics_metrics.description: When an abstract is used to support a rejection, the evidence relied upon is the facts contained in the abstract, not additional facts in the underlying full text document. Citation of an abstract without the underlying scientific document is generally inappropriate where both are prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain and analyze the underlying document; if not in English, obtain a translation so the record is clear as to precise facts relied on. The record must indicate whether reliance is on abstract or full text. Full text should normally be used to support a rejection; limited circumstances permit basing a non-final Office action on the abstract alone, but the full text and translation should be supplied in the next Office action. Whether the next action may be made final is governed by MPEP § 706.07(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 35 U.S.C. 102 (anticipation) and 103 (obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: For anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102, the reference must teach every aspect of the claimed invention explicitly or implicitly (inherently). For a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection, reference teachings must be modified to meet the claims and such modification must be one that would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§ 2131–2146 for guidance on patentability determinations under 102 and 103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining the effective filing date of the application
rubrics_metrics.description: The effective filing date may be the filing date of the application itself or, under certain circumstances, the filing date of an earlier application (parent), provisional, or may be subject to foreign priority rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claims are fully supported under 35 U.S.C. 112 by an earlier parent U.S. application, the effective filing date equals the earlier filing date. For continuation/divisional/CIP situations see MPEP §§ referenced. If claiming foreign priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) or 365(a), the effective filing date is the filing date of the U.S. application unless other situations apply. If properly claims benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) to a provisional, the effective filing date for claims fully supported by the provisional is the provisional's filing date. See MPEP §§ 1893.03(b), 201.11(a), 1895, 1895.01, 1896 for more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining the reference issue or publication date
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must determine the issue or publication date of a reference to properly compare it with the application's effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A magazine is effective as a printed publication under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as of the date it reached the addressee, not the mailing date. For foreign patents and other reference date rules see MPEP §§ 707.05(f), 901.05, 2124, 2126, 2128–2128.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying 35 U.S.C. 102(b) (statutory bar) first
rubrics_metrics.description: First consider whether a reference qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(b), since this section results in a statutory bar to obtaining a patent if the publication/issue date is more than one year prior to the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the 1-year grace period's last day falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or Federal holiday, the publication is not a statutory bar if the application was filed on the next succeeding business day (Ex parte Olah). Note that USPTO rule changes regarding deposit dates do not affect applicant's concurrent right to defer filing to next business day in such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying 35 U.S.C. 102(e) and the inventive entity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To apply a reference under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), the inventive entity of the application must be different than that of the reference. Where there are joint inventors, only one inventor need be different for inventive entities to be different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revised 35 U.S.C. 102(e) (AIPA and later amendments) applies in examination and reexamination whenever filed and is retroactive; it created prior art effect for certain publications of patent applications as of their effective U.S. filing dates. For international applications filed on or after Nov. 29, 2000, a WIPO PCT Article 21(2) English publication (with U.S. designated) may have an international filing date treated as a U.S. filing date for 102(e) purposes. International filings before Nov. 29, 2000, remain subject to the former 102(e) rules. See MPEP § 706.02(f)(1) and related discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deciding between 35 U.S.C. 102(a), (b), or (e)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once an examiner finds a printed publication or patent disclosing the claimed invention, the examiner should determine whether the rejection should be made under 35 U.S.C. 102(a), (b), or (e) by comparing the effective filing date of the application with the date of the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of the effective filing date is prerequisite. See MPEP § 706.02 for details on making the comparison and selecting the proper subsection under 102.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on abstracts vs underlying documents — evidentiary limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: If an abstract is used to support a rejection, the examiner is relying on facts in the abstract only and not on additional facts in the underlying full text document; citation of abstract alone is generally inappropriate when both abstract and underlying document are prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain copy and analyze the full text; obtain translation if not in English. The full text may reveal anticipation or teachings away that the abstract does not; the abstract may have a different effective publication date than the full text. Consider full text at earliest practicable time to improve quality and reduce pendency. If relying on abstract in a non-final action, supply full text and translation in the next Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejections in reexamination proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: For scope of rejections in reexamination proceedings, follow MPEP § 2258.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reexamination has its own scope and rules; see the referenced MPEP section for details.
